---
name: storyfolio
description: Use when someone wants a personal portfolio site made from their profile, resume, LinkedIn or GitHub, especially one with 3D, scroll-driven animation or a story, or says their portfolio looks generic, templated or AI-made.
---

# Storyfolio

Makes one kind of portfolio site: one long scroll that tells one story, carried by one object in 3D that is taken from the person's own work.

This version plans the site and does not build it. It ends when the person has said yes to a storyboard.

## Three stops

Between stops you work by yourself. At each stop the person decides one thing. You go on only when their answer is in the conversation and you have written it into the file.

| Stop | First open | You put to the person | You go on when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Read | `references/reading-a-profile.md` | What you found, as facts to confirm and questions to answer. Nothing else | They have answered, and `docs/story/facts.md` holds their answers |
| 2. Concept | `references/concept.md` | Three concepts, and which you would choose | They have picked one, or told you to pick, and `docs/story/concepts.md` says which |
| 3. Storyboard | `references/storyboard.md` | The script of the whole page | They have said yes to it |

**Your first reply is the first stop, and no more than that.** People ask for the whole plan at once: the idea, the scroll, the colours. Do not give it yet, and say why in a sentence. A plan made now is made from your reading of a resume, and a resume leaves out exactly what a site must not get wrong: whose result a number was, what a title hides, who took a photograph. Once they have answered you will have a better idea, and it will not have to be taken apart.

When the storyboard has its yes, say that building is not in this version, and bring `docs/story/handover.md` up to date.

## Ask or decide

Ask the person when a thing is:

1. a fact only they know,
2. a claim that could embarrass them if it were wrong,
3. taste on what a visitor sees first: the concept, the look, the opening words,
4. anything that publishes, costs money, or shows another person or an employer's work.

Everything else you decide. Write each decision into `docs/story/decided-for-you.md`: what you decided, why, and how to change it.

If the person will not answer, or tells you to decide everything, open `references/asking.md`.

## What you keep

In the person's own folder, so that a later session can go on from the files alone:

| File | Holds |
|---|---|
| `docs/story/facts.md` | The fact sheet, each fact with where it came from, and the person's answers |
| `docs/story/concepts.md` | The three concepts, which was picked, and why |
| `docs/story/storyboard.md` | The script |
| `docs/story/decided-for-you.md` | What you decided without asking |
| `docs/story/handover.md` | What exists, what the person has said, what is next |

## What holds from the first stop on

- **Nothing about the person is invented.** You know that a number, an employer, a title and a quote are facts. So is every small thing a sentence says on its way: what was wrong before they came, how often a thing is used, which came first, why, how a thing was left, what it taught them. That sounds like writing, and it is a claim. Before you hand anything over, read each sentence about the person and find the line of the fact sheet it stands on. A sentence with no line goes, or becomes a question.
- **A number is used as the person confirmed it,** with what it measures and whose result it is.
- **What is someone else's is asked about before it is planned for:** a photograph a photographer took, a friend's drawing, a quote, an employer's screens, a story with a patient or a client in it.

# Reading a profile

The first stop. You read everything, write down what you found, and ask. You do not plan yet.

## What to read

Everything the person gave you: a resume, a LinkedIn profile, GitHub, writing, talks, notes to you, a site they already have. Read all of it before you write a word.

A site they already have is a source of facts and pictures. What becomes of it is theirs to say, so ask.

## LinkedIn

You cannot fetch a LinkedIn profile. It turns away anything that is not signed in. It reaches you in one of four ways:

- **A PDF.** On their own profile, in a desktop browser: **More** under their name (some accounts show **Resources**), then **Save to PDF**. The phone app does not have it.
- **A copy of their data.** **Me**, **Settings & Privacy**, **Data privacy**, **Get a copy of your data**. They can pick only the profile and the positions, and the link then comes by email within minutes. The whole archive can take a day.
- **The text,** pasted.
- **Their own browser,** where you have a tool that works it and they have said yes.

These steps were checked against LinkedIn's help pages on 10 October 2026. The names of its buttons change.

**A copy of their data holds more than a profile.** It has their messages, and everyone they are connected to. Those are other people's words and addresses. The person unzipped a folder: they did not hand you their inbox. Open the files that are about the profile: the profile, positions, education, skills, projects, honours, recommendations. Leave messages and connections unopened, and tell the person that you left them. Nothing from the archive goes into the repository but facts about the person.

## The fact sheet

Write `docs/story/facts.md`. Beside every fact, write where it came from.

- **Who they are,** in the words they use for themselves.
- **Where they have been,** with the years.
- **Each job:** the employer, the title, the dates, what they did there.
- **Each project:** what it was, what they did in it, who else did, what there is to show of it.
- **Each figure.**
- **What others have said** of them.
- **What they learned from:** a book, a person, a first failure.
- **Each picture, drawing or file** they say they have.

## What one source hides

Where two sources disagree, you will see it. The mistakes that reach a site are in one line of one resume, where nothing disagrees with it. A team's result reads as theirs. A lab's name suggests work they never did. A photograph has someone else in it.

So put these to every line of the fact sheet. Where the material does not answer, you have a question for the person.

| Of every | Ask |
|---|---|
| Figure | What does it measure, and over what time? Is it measured, modelled or a guess? Whose result is it: theirs, or a team's? |
| Result of a team, a firm or a club | Were they in it when it happened, and what was their part? |
| Job, employer or lab | What did they themselves do there, in a sentence of their own? Its name is not an answer, and neither is a line such as "operations" or "supported the team". |
| Project | What was it: something in use, a course exercise, a script? Did it ever run anywhere? Who else made it? |
| Title | Is it what they are on paper, or what they are called? |
| Picture, drawing or quote | Who made it? Whose is it to use? Who or what does it show? |
| Story about a patient, a client or a colleague | May it be told at all, and with what left out? |
| Anything of an employer's | May it be shown? |

End the fact sheet with three lists:

- **Gaps.** What a site needs and the material lacks: a project with no picture, a job with no outcome.
- **Disagreements.** Where two sources differ, with both readings. You do not settle one yourself, and you do not take the one that reads better.
- **To confirm.** Every question the table raised.

## What you put to the person

One message, which is the whole of your reply:

1. Two or three sentences on who you take them to be.
2. Your questions, numbered, so that they can answer by number. Plain words. Say why you ask wherever that is not plain. Every disagreement and every item under "To confirm" is one of them.
3. These, which no material answers:
   - Who is the site for, and what should a visitor do when they reach its end?
   - What must not be shown?
   - What do you work from, day to day? The documents, lists and rituals of your trade, by the names you call them.
   - What did you learn from?
   - If they have a site already: what becomes of it?
4. Nothing else. No concept, no outline, no look.

When they answer, write each answer into the fact sheet beside its fact, before you do anything else.

Every question then stands as one of two: answered, in their words, or not answered. One they passed over is not answered, and it stays under "To confirm". Silence is not a yes. That they have photographs does not say whose the photographs are.

Some notes from me (Ines)

Pictures I have:
- about 60 photos of dishes and the jar wall, taken by Priya Nair for the
  restaurant's website
- my own phone photos of the larder, labels and all
- scans of all four issues of Brine (drawings by my friend Olu)
- a photo of my grandmother's ogiri pot

Things people ask me about: the jar wall, the koji room (it is a cupboard),
the staff meal, and the workshops I run on the first Monday of the month.

I took over the kitchen in September 2022.

Books that got me here: The Art of Fermentation by Sandor Katz, and Wild
Fermentation. And my grandmother, who never measured anything.
(Saved from LinkedIn as text, October 2026)

Ines Okafor
Head Chef at Saltmarsh. Fermentation, whole-vegetable cooking, apprentices.
Leeds, England, United Kingdom

ABOUT
I cook at Saltmarsh, a 40-seat restaurant in Leeds. Most of what I care about
happens before service: what we do with the trim, the whey, the stems and the
bones. We have a wall of jars and a prep list that is longer than the menu.
I run our apprentice programme and write a small zine about preserving,
called Brine.

EXPERIENCE

Head Chef, Saltmarsh, Leeds
Mar 2022 to present
- A menu that changes every week
- Cut kitchen food waste from 14 kg to 5 kg a week
- Built the larder: 40+ ferments, vinegars and garums on rotation
- Two apprentices a year since 2023

Sous Chef, The Corn Exchange Kitchen, Leeds
Jun 2019 to Feb 2022
- Ran the pass on a 90-cover service
- Took over ordering and brought the supplier list from 31 to 12

Chef de Partie, Brassica, Manchester
Sep 2016 to May 2019
- Larder and garnish, then sauce

Fjaerland Fermentation Lab, Norway
Jan 2018 to Mar 2018

EDUCATION
Leeds Kitchen College. Diploma in Professional Cookery, 2014 to 2016

VOLUNTEERING
Sunday Pot, Leeds. Co-founder. 2021 to present
A hot meal every Sunday at St Aidan's hall, cooked from what restaurants in
the city have left over.

PUBLICATIONS
Brine. A zine about preserving. Four issues, 2022 to 2025.

RECOMMENDATIONS
Callum Reyes, owner of Saltmarsh:
"Ines turned our bins into a larder. The best thing on the menu most weeks
started as something we used to throw away."

I’ll record those corrections and use your judgment instruction to carry the plan through. I’m continuing with the storyfolio skill; I’ll read its guidance for delegated decisions before choosing the concept and writing the full storyboard.


The ferment log gives the site its structure: start a record, check it, establish readiness, then write the menu. I’ve chosen that over a prep-list concept because it gives the scroll a clear purpose. The storyboard also keeps the waste result credited to the whole kitchen and describes Fjaerland explicitly as a stage.


I’ve chosen **The ferment log**: a continuous story answering **“What happens before the menu is written?”** The full plan is in [storyboard.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-chef-with-Vei34y/docs/story/storyboard.md). Nothing has been built.

Before publication, these remain open:

1. Your public contact details and workshop/application destinations.
2. The actual photographs you own.
3. Restaurant permission for Priya’s photographs, with her credit; Olu’s permission for his drawings. The plan works without either.
4. Any staff consent needed for chosen images. Supplier prices stay excluded.

**The idea**

Six paper leaves from an interpreted ferment log carry the experience. As you scroll, they separate into a chronology, align into working fields, open into an evidence grid, compare the waste measurements, then gather again.

The same object stays throughout. Its movement helps visitors follow your work: recording, checking, inspecting and deciding what is ready. Your statement that the menu is written last gives the story its ending.

I considered a prep-list bundle and a set of jar-label sleeves. The log offers the strongest complete story using what you have already confirmed. All three are recorded in [concepts.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-chef-with-Vei34y/docs/story/concepts.md).

**The scroll, top to bottom**

| Chapter | What visitors see | What moves |
|---|---|---|
| **Started** | Your name, role, central question, and influences: your grandmother and the fermentation books. Your pot photograph anchors the opening when supplied. | A shallow stack opens, revealing the first leaves. |
| **Date** | Your career, including the ten-week unpaid stage and its actual tasks. Acting head chef and formal Head Chef dates remain distinct. | The leaves spread into a dated sequence; the stage record comes forward briefly. |
| **Salt** | The prep list and ferment-log fields: start date, salt, check days, readiness. Then the menu, written last. | The leaves align into a readable working spread. No invented entries or recipes. |
| **Checks** | Your larder and labels, the koji cupboard, apprentice programme, workshops, Brine and Sunday Pot. | The leaves form a grid; an owned photograph can expand for inspection. |
| **Ready** | The kitchen’s waste result and Callum’s quotation. The figures retain “we,” the one-month measurement in 2023, prep-and-plate scope and exclusion of bones. | Two leaves present the figures together; another reveals the quotation. |
| **Next batch** | Three clear routes: apprentice enquiries, workshop enquiries/bookings, and contact for food writers. | The leaves return to a complete stack. |

The desktop story takes roughly eight to nine screens, with ordinary scrolling. A chapter rail and immediate enquiry link let visitors move directly to what matters. The first screen also contains your identity, practice and a compact, properly qualified proof point.

**Colour and type**

I chose warm log paper **#F2EBDD**, dark ink **#252A24**, and olive **#46563D**. The leaves have subtle rules, matte surfaces and soft shadows.

**Source Sans 3** handles readable text and headings; **IBM Plex Mono** handles dates, log fields and measurements. No imitation handwriting or manufactured stains. Two alternative palette studies are documented for later comparison.

**On a phone**

The site becomes a single readable column. Dates run vertically; evidence becomes stacked cards. Small phones use static chapter illustrations, with no prolonged pinned scene or compulsory animation.

Reduced-motion mode removes the moving transitions. Without WebGL or JavaScript, visitors still get the complete text, evidence, navigation and contact links. The 3D never controls access to information.

**What else it needs**

The plan includes accessible navigation, image descriptions, credits, share previews, search metadata, a missing-page screen and privacy information appropriate to the eventual contact setup. Images load responsively; the readable page appears before the 3D.

I assumed English, enquiry-based contact until booking details exist, and a concise work index. Separate project pages, a blog and payment handling can follow when there is material or an operational need. I left out a CV, chat and tracking. All assumptions are recorded in [decided-for-you.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-chef-with-Vei34y/docs/story/decided-for-you.md).

**Does this storyboard have your yes, or what would you change?**

The [storyfolio skill](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-chef-with-Vei34y/.agents/skills/storyfolio/SKILL.md) ends with “The script of the whole page” and requires “They have said yes to it.” This is the final planning checkpoint; approval does not trigger a build.

# Asking

## Facts

At the first stop your questions go in one message, numbered. `reading-a-profile.md` says what they are.

## A choice

Where you offer a choice, the concept above all, give the ones you would not choose as fully as the one you would. Then say which you would choose, and why.

If the person tells you to choose, choose. Write what you chose, and what you chose it over, into `docs/story/decided-for-you.md`.

## If the person will not answer

Some people will not answer your questions, or will say: decide everything. Then:

- **What is a matter of taste, you decide:** the concept, the look, the order. Say which you chose and what you chose it over.
- **A fact, you do not decide.** What you could not confirm stays off the page. A figure whose meaning you do not know, a project you cannot say ever ran, a paper you cannot say they wrote, a title you cannot say is theirs: leave it out, or carry it in the script marked "to confirm", and stand nothing on it. Build the concept on the facts that needed no confirming. The person's own resume is no exception: if you asked whether a project ever ran and they did not say, "real-time system" is still not confirmed, and it is not printed.
- **Say what is waiting on them,** as a numbered list at the top of what you hand over.

A wrong guess about someone's taste costs them an afternoon. A wrong claim about their work is read by the people they most want to convince, and it is their name on the site, not yours.
# The concept

The second stop: from the fact sheet to three concepts the person can choose between.

## What does not work

- A new coat of paint on the same sections.
- 3D as a backdrop behind the text.
- One 3D scene, however good.
- Another site's idea with the names changed.
- A different effect for every section: a wall of jars, then a door that opens, then a scale that tips. Each may be good. Together they are a tour of effects, and nothing carries the visitor from the first to the last.

## Three things to find

**One question.** The page answers it, and the last screen gives the answer. Look where two sides of the person's work meet, or in the way from one thing to another, or in what all their projects circle. Word it as someone in HR would say it and a colleague would respect. It is about something that interests the person now, and it claims nothing the fact sheet does not hold.

Write it as a question, with a question mark. "Teardown" and "Signal from noise" are themes: they give a page a mood. A question gives the page somewhere to go, and gives the ending a job.

**One form.** A document or a ritual of the person's own trade that already runs from a beginning to an end, with section names a colleague would know: a paper, a runbook, a job card, a shift handover, a set of drawings. List at least five that the trade has, and take one the person said they work from. Its section names become the chapters, in its order, and no jokes are made in its voice. A chapter holds what its name says.

"Hero, About, Work, Skills, Contact" is the form of a website. It belongs to nobody.

**One object.** The thing that form is physically made of, in five to twelve similar pieces. The pieces carry the person's real work on their faces. They are recognisable standing together at rest. They can be built from simple shapes. They are on screen from the first screen to the last.

The object comes from what the person makes. It is not the trade's emblem: a chef's hat, a server rack, a stethoscope. For anyone who works with data, the emblem is a field of points that gathers into a chart. It fits every analyst alive, which is what is wrong with it.

## What every form has to hold

Map the form's sections onto these roles. Leave out a role that has nothing to hold. Five to eight chapters. Someone with little to show yet gets a shorter story, and not a padded one.

| Role | Holds |
|---|---|
| The opening | Their name, and the question |
| Who | Who is asking |
| Where from | The places and the years |
| How | The way they work |
| What | Some of the work shown working, then all of it |
| What came of it | Outcomes |
| What others say | Their words, one at a time |
| The close | The answer, and how to reach them |

## What the object becomes

In each chapter the same pieces take a new arrangement that shows what the chapter is about: the way they came as a line or a map, how they work as a diagram, one piece of work as an exhibit, every project as a wall whose faces carry real pictures, outcomes as cards. At the close the object is whole again.

If a chapter's 3D could be deleted and only decoration would be lost, the pieces are not showing that chapter yet.

**The opening shows where the object comes from.** The answer is the person's own: what they learned from, or what they began with. The object may gather, be put together, unfold, be drawn, develop or switch on.

## Three concepts, each written like this

Make three that differ in kind: in their form or their object, and not in their colour. Write them to `docs/story/concepts.md`.

- **The question.**
- **The form,** with each chapter's name and the role it holds.
- **The object,** and its pieces.
- **What it becomes** in three of the chapters.
- **The opening and the close.**
- **What it stands on:** the lines of the fact sheet it needs.
- **What it needs from the person:** a picture, someone else's yes.
- **Why it is theirs:** one sentence on why it could not sit on a colleague's site.

Then say which you would choose, and why.

## Test each one before you show it

Rework or drop one that fails.

| Test | Ask |
|---|---|
| Swap | Could it sit unchanged on a colleague's site? Then it is not theirs yet. |
| Backdrop | With the 3D deleted, is meaning lost, or only decoration? |
| Depth | Has it a beginning, a middle and an end that follow from one another? |
| Emblem | Is the object the picture that stands for the job? |
| Honesty | Does any sentence in it say more than the fact sheet does: a ranking, a reason, which came first, how a thing was left, a day, a place? |
| Thirty seconds | Can someone who does not scroll get the name, the work, some proof, and how to reach them? |

## Three cases

How each was reasoned, and not only where it ended.

**A research paper.** The site this skill came from belongs to someone whose work lies between AI research and software engineering. Three restyled layouts were, in their words, "all cliche". Three single 3D scenes were "not deep enough". What turned it was a sentence of theirs: "Think of it like a research question." The form became a paper, with a paper's chapters: Abstract, Introduction, Background, Method, Experiments, Results, Peer review, Conclusion. The object became the paper's nine pages, which fold into a globe for where they have lived, stand as the layers of a network for how they work, and hang as a wall of projects. The question was first too abstract for a recruiter, and was reworded. The opening was first a plain pile of pages. It became the front pages of the papers they learned from, gathering into the paper as the reader scrolls.

**A tasting menu.** Camille is a pastry chef, made up for this page. She trained in Lyon, spent six years in the pastry sections of two restaurants, and now runs a dessert-only evening once a month: 24 seats, five courses, all sweet. People write to her about one burnt-honey tart. Her trade's forms: the recipe card, the prep list, the tasting menu, the order sheet, the costing sheet. She serves in courses and plans by the menu, so the form is a tasting menu, and each course is a chapter. Each course arrives on a plate, so the object is a stack of plates. The question: "What makes someone remember a dessert?" Turned down first: a whisk and a chef's hat turning in the air, which is the emblem, and one croissant in 3D, which is one scene.

**An incident review.** Jun is a reliability engineer, also made up. Seven years on call, at a payments company and then at one that books hospital appointments. He wrote his team's incident review template, and gives talks on reviews without blame. His trade's forms: the runbook, the incident review, the on-call handover, the status page, the dashboard. His work is what happens after something breaks, so the form is an incident review: summary, timeline, root cause, action items. A status page is made of tiles, one to a service, so the object is those tiles. The question: "What keeps a system up at 3 a.m.?" Turned down first: a server rack turning, which is the emblem, and a globe of pings behind the text, which is a backdrop.

**An example shows how to reason. Its concept is not taken.** Camille's menu was reasoned from how Camille serves. A chef who sells one loaf a day from a hatch is not a tasting menu. If you find one of these three concepts in your hand for someone else, it has already failed the swap test: it was made for a person who is not in front of you.

In this version a concept is shown in words. There is no engine yet to sketch one on.
# The storyboard

The third stop: the script of the whole page, which the person says yes to. Write it to `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

A plan covers what its asker thought to ask for. Most people ask for the idea and for what moves. Nobody asks what the site does on a phone, or without the 3D, or what a shared link shows, and a script that leaves those out is half a script. So this one has a place for each, and an empty place shows.

## The chapters

A row to a chapter:

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What it tells, in a few words | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## The beats

Under each chapter, a row to a beat. A beat is one settled state of the scene and one block of text.

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | What its caption stands on |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Screens:** how much scroll the beat takes. One, or more where the scroll works something.
- **How the pieces stand:** a stack, a fan, a ring, a row, a wall, or what the chapter needs. The same pieces in every beat.
- **What is on their faces:** the person's real pictures and words. Name the picture.
- **What the chapter adds:** anything in the scene besides the pieces. Often nothing.
- **What its caption stands on:** a working title of a few words, and the lines of the fact sheet the caption will be written from. Not the caption.

**Write no captions yet.** The words are written at a later stop, where the person chooses them. **3. Salt — how the kitchen works**

Approximately 1½ screens.

| Field | What the section explains |
|---|---|
